title: China’s New Laws Are Ensnaring Western Companies
gist: Since 2020 China has built an expanding legal toolkit (Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law, Blocking Rules, Counter-Extraterritorial Regulation) that lets Chinese courts sue and penalize foreign companies for complying with Western sanctions, meaning multinationals can no longer treat overcompliance with U.S./EU sanctions as the 'safe' default — every sanctions-driven contract decision now risks legal exposure in China as well as the West.

insights.claim: China has built a stack of countersanctions laws since 2020 — the Export Control Law (2020), Unreliable Entity List (2020), Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law (2021), Blocking Rules (2021), Counter-Extraterritorial Regulation (2026), and Supply Chain Security Provisions (2026) — that collectively let Beijing penalize companies for complying with foreign sanctions while asserting its own extraterritorial jurisdiction.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: Any multinational operating in or with China now needs a distinct, dedicated legal-risk workstream for Chinese countersanctions exposure separate from Western sanctions compliance — a new structural cost for China-exposed supply chains.
insights.quote: The resulting legal environment puts foreign companies in a bind: They can face legal exposure in the West for violating Western sanctions—and in China for complying with them.

insights.claim: Article 12 of China's Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law gives Chinese individuals and entities a private right to sue any person or company that implements or assists in implementing foreign restrictive measures that harm Chinese interests — effectively letting Chinese counterparties sue Western firms for refusing to perform contracts on sanctions grounds.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: This creates litigation risk for any Western firm that terminates or withholds performance on a China-linked contract citing sanctions — legal teams need to price this into every China-exposed contract with a sanctions carve-out clause.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Designed as an instrument of self-defense'

insights.claim: In the first reported Article 12 case (Nanjing Maritime Court, 2024), a Chinese offshore engineering contractor obtained a preservation order arresting a vessel after a Swiss counterparty withheld nearly $12 million in payments citing sanctions concerns; the dispute was resolved via court-brokered mediation after the Swiss firm secured a U.S. sanctions exemption, demonstrating Article 12's practical leverage even without a final judgment.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence Chinese courts can seize foreign assets (vessels) to pressure Western counterparties back to the table over sanctions-related payment disputes — a real operational risk for shipping, offshore engineering, and any capital-intensive China-linked contract.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The first reported case involving Article 12'

insights.claim: In 2025 the Shanghai Maritime Court ruled against a Singaporean shipping firm that refused to deliver goods to a Hong Kong manufacturer after the manufacturer was placed on the U.S. entity list, holding that the refusal constituted implementing 'foreign discriminatory restrictive measures'; China's Supreme People's Court included this among six representative maritime cases published in June 2026, signaling how Chinese courts will approach similar disputes.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: This ruling establishes binding-precedent-like guidance that refusing to deal with a U.S.-sanctioned Chinese/Hong Kong counterparty can itself trigger Chinese legal liability — a direct threat to the 'de-risk by refusing transactions' playbook.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'A second case before the Shanghai Maritime Court'

insights.claim: In May 2026 Beijing triggered its Blocking Rules for the first time, prohibiting five Chinese petrochemical 'teapot' refineries, including Hengli Petrochemical Refinery, from complying with U.S. sanctions over their alleged purchases of Iranian oil — a carefully calibrated test using firms with limited U.S. financial-system exposure and nondollar payment channels.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: This is a controlled pilot; the real test — and bigger market risk — comes when Blocking Rules are applied to larger, globally integrated Chinese firms with genuine dollar-system exposure.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'In May, Beijing triggered the Blocking Rules'

insights.claim: China's Ministry of Justice issued its first formal Counter-Extraterritorial Regulation determination in May 2026, ruling that the European Commission's anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese security firm Nuctech under the EU Foreign Subsidies Regulation constituted improper extraterritorial jurisdiction — a direct jurisdictional clash because the disputed data was stored on the parent company's China-based servers.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: EU regulatory investigations into Chinese-owned firms with China-hosted data now risk direct jurisdictional counterattack from Beijing — relevant to EU antitrust/subsidy enforcement against Chinese companies operating in Europe.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'In May, China's Ministry of Justice issued'

insights.claim: Two Chinese energy firm lawsuits against Citigroup (Shanghai court, February 2026) and JPMorgan Chase (Beijing court, one month later) over frozen payments tied to U.S. sanctions concerns — involving a modest $40.5 million disputed amount but a potentially significant precedent — show global banks are now direct litigation targets for de-risking decisions.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: Global banks (Citigroup, JPMorgan) face a live, ongoing litigation precedent risk in China for routine sanctions-compliance freezes — a new line-item legal/compliance cost for Western banks with China operations.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Two recent cases involving global banks'

themes.theme: Strategic asymmetry vs. Russia parallel and payment-system workaround

insights.claim: China's extraterritorial reach differs structurally from the U.S.'s: Washington's leverage rests on dollar-system centrality and tech leadership, while China lacks equivalent financial leverage and instead is building chokepoints in critical minerals, supply chains, market access, and data — powerful but narrower than the dollar system.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: Investors should not expect Chinese extraterritorial sanctions power to rival U.S. dollar-based sanctions reach broadly — but sector-specific chokepoints (critical minerals, rare earths, supply chains) remain a targeted lever worth tracking for those sectors.

insights.claim: China is simultaneously promoting alternative payment channels — its CIPS system (an alternative to SWIFT), the mBridge multilateral central bank digital currency platform, and digital yuan pilots — to reduce vulnerability to financial coercion, though these do not yet rival the dollar system's reach.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: CIPS/mBridge/digital yuan adoption is a slow-moving but structural de-dollarization trend worth monitoring for long-term implications on dollar-denominated trade settlement and sanctions enforceability.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'At the same time, China is seeking'

insights.claim: China's approach mirrors Russia's playbook of channeling sanctions-related disputes into domestic courts since 2020, producing predictable outcomes that often disregard contractual dispute-resolution clauses — with Beijing's own Communist Party-controlled courts now central to its economic lawfare strategy.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: The EU's post-2022 defensive toolkit developed against Russian court retaliation (blocking enforcement of foreign judgments, allowing loss recovery) is a template the author says could become 'increasingly relevant' for China exposure — a preview of coming EU regulatory response.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'With its insistence on jurisdiction'

insights.claim: Multinationals can no longer assume overcompliance with U.S. or EU sanctions is the safest option; a single business decision — such as terminating a contract with a Chinese supplier to comply with U.S. export controls — can now trigger cumulative exposure across the Unreliable Entity List, Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law measures, Blocking Rules scrutiny, Counter-Extraterritorial Regulation investigation, and civil lawsuits, with some instruments raising personal liability risk for executives in China.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: This is the article's central actionable thesis: compliance teams must now run a two-sided risk assessment on every China-linked sanctions decision, and contractual sanctions clauses may no longer reliably shield firms — a structural increase in legal/compliance cost for any China-exposed multinational.
insights.quote: The key question for companies is no longer simply whether they are exposed to U.S. or EU sanctions risk. It is whether any response to that risk creates liability in China.

insights.claim: Following the Shanghai Maritime Court decision, standard contractual sanctions clauses may no longer reliably protect companies, since a Chinese court can now treat nonperformance under such a clause as itself implementing foreign restrictive measures against a Chinese counterparty.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: Legacy sanctions-clause boilerplate in China-linked contracts may be legally ineffective in China going forward, a material drafting/risk-management gap for corporate counsel.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Until recently, adding broadly drafted sanctions clauses'

insights.claim: European companies face a uniquely difficult three-way squeeze, since they already navigate overlapping EU and U.S. sanctions regimes and now face a third jurisdiction (China) pulling in another direction, with the EU's own blocking statute offering limited protection, especially for firms with assets, personnel, counterparties, or data in China.
insights.speaker: Maria Shagina
insights.so_what: European multinationals with China exposure face the most acute version of this three-jurisdiction compliance bind — a distinct risk factor versus U.S.-only or China-only exposed peers.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'European companies face a particularly difficult position'
